Was there SAMBA in Columbia? Paleomagnetic evidence from
1790 Ma Avanavero mafic sills (northern Amazonian Craton)
Franklin Bispo-Santosa,∗, Manoel S. D’Agrella-Filhoa, Ricardo I.F. Trindadea,
Liliane Janikianb, Nelson J. Reisc
aInstituto de Astronomia, Geofísica e Ciências Atmosféricas, Universidade de São Paulo, Rua do Matão, 1226, São Paulo, SP 05508-090, Brazil
bUniversidade Católica de Santos, Av. Conselheiro Nébias 300, Vila Mathias, Santos, SP 11015-002, Brazil
cGeological Survey of Brazil, Manaus Agency, Av. André Araújo 2160, Manaus, Amazonas, Brazil
a r t i c l e i n f o
Article history:
Received 16 February 2013
Received in revised form 7 November 2013
Accepted 10 November 2013
Available online 21 November 2013
Keywords:
Paleomagnetism
Avanavero sills
Amazonian Craton
Columbia
a
Supercontinent
b s t r a c t
The Amazonian Craton represents an important piece in the Paleoproterozoic paleogeography of the
Earth. This study presents paleomagnetic data obtained on well-dated (U–Pb) 1790 Ma mafic sills from
the Avanavero magmatism in northern Amazonian Craton (Guiana Shield). AF and thermal treatments
revealed southeastern, low downward/upward inclination, remanent magnetization directions that are
carried by moderate to high-Hcand high-TBTi-poor titanomagnetite. The site mean directions cluster
around the mean Dm= 138.2◦, Im= −3.4◦(N = 13, ˛ 95= 13.0◦), which yields a robust paleomagnetic pole
(AV pole) at 27.9◦E, 48.4◦S (A95= 9.6◦) with a Q-value of 5. The characteristic component disclosed for the
Avanavero sill matches that obtained for sediments collected along the baked contact and are distinct from
those away from the sill. The Avanavero directions are also significantly different from those obtained for
younger units, with ages spanning from 1420 to 520 Ma, suggesting the sills carry a primary remanence.
The Avanavero pole helps in constraining the paleogeography of the central pieces of Columbia. It is
compatible with the Baltica and Amazonian Cratons SAMBA link in the Columbia Supercontinent at about
1780 Ma, but other configurations are also possible. When compared to other Paleo- to Mesoproterozoic
paleomagnetic poles from the southern Amazonian Craton (Central Brazil Shield), our new paleomagnetic
pole suggests intracratonic motions within the southern area of the Craton, probably after 1420 Ma ago.
We tentatively suggest that these movements are related to the collision of the Paraguá Block with the
proto-Amazonian Craton at about 1350–1320 Ma ago.

1. Introduction
The paleogeography of Proterozoic supercontinents is still con-
troversial because of the difficulties and uncertainties that arise
when someone compares the geological and geophysical record
of continental fragments that once have come together to form
them (Pesonen et al., 2003). Nevertheless, it is believed that at least
twice in the Proterozoic continents assembled to form superconti-
nents (Hossain et al., 2007): at ca. 1850 Ma ago with the Columbia
Supercontinent (e.g., Rogers, 1996; Rogers and Santosh, 2002; Zhao
et al., 2004, 2006, 2008; Meert, 2012; Kusky et al., 2007; Johansson,
2009; Yakubchuk, 2010), and at ca. 1100–1000 Ma with the Rodinia
supercontinent (e.g., Hoffman, 1991; Dalziel, 1997; Weil et al.,
1998; D’Agrella-Filho et al., 1998; Pesonen et al., 2003; Li et al.,
2008; Evans, 2009).
∗
Corresponding author. Tel.: +55 11984630126.
E-mail addresses: frankb@iag.usp.br, franklin bs@hotmail.com (F.
The
Bispo-Santos).
exact configuration of Columbia is still unknown and a
great deal of geological, geochronological and paleomagnetic data
is required in order to provide a means of establishing the links
between the different continental fragments in the Paleo- and
Mesoproterozoic. From the paleomagnetic point of view, only pre-
cisely dated Paleoproterozoic geological units of these continental
fragments have the potential to provide reliable information to con-
strain the Columbia paleogeography (Buchan et al., 2000; Pesonen
et al., 2003). Gradually, these data are being acquired in sev-
eral continents and we can now propose some crude quantitative
tests on the different Columbia configurations using the paleo-
magnetic database (e.g., Meert, 2002, 2012; Pesonen et al., 2003,
2012; Salminen and Pesonen, 2007; Bispo-Santos et al., 2008, 2012;
Johansson, 2009; Cordani et al., 2009; Lubnina et al., 2010; Piper
et al., 2011; Evans and Mitchell, 2011; Zhang et al., 2012; D’Agrella-
Filho et al., 2012; Mertanen and Pesonen, 2012).
Baltica and Laurentia are the central pieces of Columbia. There
are basically two models for the Laurentia-Baltica connection in
this supercontinent: the first one juxtaposes western Baltica to
the southeastern Greenland in Laurentia (Zhao et al., 2004; Hou
0301-9268/$ – see front matter © 2013 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved.
http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.precamres.2013.11.002

geochronological Provinces (after Tassinari et al., 2000); (b) general geometry of SW Amazonian Craton showing the ca. 1.47–1.35 Ga Alto Guaporé belt (Rizzotto and
Hartmann, 2012), and the ca. 1.2–1.0 Ga Sunsás, Aguapeí and Nova Brasilândia belts (adapted from D’Agrella-Filho et al., 2012); (c) schematic stratigraphic section of Roraima
Supergroup in the studied area (after Reis and Yánez, 2001).
et al., 2008; Johansson, 2009; Halls et al., 2011), the second one
juxtaposes northern Baltica to eastern Greenland (Karlstrom et al.,
2001; Buchan et al., 2000; Pesonen et al., 2003; Zhao et al., 2006;
Salminen and Pesonen, 2007; Lubnina et al., 2010; Pisarevsky
and Bylund, 2010; Evans and Mitchell, 2011; D’Agrella-Filho
et al., 2012; Bispo-Santos et al., 2008, 2012). Paleomagnetic
evidence favors the last link (Buchan et al., 2000; Salminen and
Pesonen, 2007; Lubnina et al., 2010; Pisarevsky and Bylund, 2010).
Also at the heart of Columbia, a link between northern South
America (SAM) (Amazonian Craton) and southwestern Baltica
(BA), dubbed SAMBA, was proposed on the basis of Archaean to
Paleo-Mesoproterozoic geological evidence (e.g., Johansson, 2009).
However, until recently the available Paleo- to Mesoproterozoic
paleomagnetic data implied a gap between these two blocks
(Pesonen et al., 2003; Bispo-Santos et al., 2008; D’Agrella-Filho
et al., 2012). Based on 1790–1770 Ma paleomagnetic data from
Baltica (Ropruchey sills and Shoksha Formation), Amazonian Cra-
ton (Colíder Group) and North China (Tahiang dykes), Bispo-Santos
et al. (2008) suggested that North China could fill the gap between
Baltica and the Amazonian Craton. Recent paleomagnetic data from
1420 Ma mafic dykes from Nova Guarita swarm and gabbros from
the Indiavaí Intrusive (southern Amazonian Craton) seemed to
corroborate this interpretation (D’Agrella-Filho et al., 2012). Here
we present a paleomagnetic study of well-dated 1789 Ma mafic
sills from the Avanavero magmatic event located at the northern
Roraima State (Central Amazonian Province of the Amazonian
Craton) and its implications for the paleogeography of
2.
Columbia.
Geological setting
The Amazonian Craton (Fig. 1a) is one of the largest stable
cratonic areas in the world (430,000 km2). It is exposed in two
large areas separated by the Phanerozoic Amazonian sedimentary
basin comprising the northern Guiana Shield and the south-
ern Central-Brazil or Guaporé Shield (Lacerda-Filho et al., 2004;
Schobbenhaus et al., 1984; Santos et al., 2000). Its northeastern
part consists of two Archean nuclei (>2600 Ma – Central Amazo-
nian Province in Fig. 1a) encircled by a predominantly accretionary
Paleoproterozoic belt (2250–2050 Ma) which form the Maroni-
Itacaiúnas Province (Tassinari and Macambira, 1999; Tassinari
et al., 2000). The southwestern part of this Archean nucleus
was accreted by subduction-related juvenile magmatic arcs form-
ing the 1980–1810 Ma Ventuari-Tapajós, and the 1780–1600 Ma
Rio Negro-Juruena Provinces (Tassinari et al., 2000; Pinho et al.,
2003; Schobbenhaus and Brito-Neves, 2003; Cordani and Teixeira,
2007). In the Mesoproterozoic, subduction-related magmatic arcs
of the 1600–1300 Ma Jauru Terrane in the Central-Brazil Shield
(Rondonian-San Ignacio Province) developed until the final colli-
sion of the Paraguá Terrane at ca. 1320 Ma (Bettencourt et al., 2010).
This collisional model was recently extended to the northwest
with the recognition of the Trincheira ophiolite by Rizzotto and
Hartmann (2012). These authors interpret these rocks as a record
of oceanic crust relics associated with the collision of the Paraguá
Block with the proto-Amazonian Craton along the Alto Guaporé
Belt at the Middle Mesoproterozoic (Fig. 1b). In this geotectonic

### page_3
F. Bispo-Santos et al. / Precambrian Research 244 (2014) 139–155 141
scenario the E-W 1100–1000 Ma Nova Brasilândia belt (NBB)
located between the proto-Amazonian Craton and the Paraguá
block, and once interpreted as a suture zone between these two
cratonic blocks (Tohver et al., 2004), most probably represents
intracratonic reactivations occurred during the development of the
Greenvile-type 1200–950 Ma Sunsás-Aguapeí Belt (e.g., Teixeira
et al., 2010). Similar 1420 Ma paleomagnetic poles obtained for
the Nova Guarita dykes and the Indiavaí intrusive, whose areas are
located on opposite sides of the NBB, corroborate this intracratonic
interpretation (D’Agrella-Filho et al., 2012).
The study area is located in the Central Amazonian Province
(CAP; Fig. 1a), which is composed of Archaean continental crust
(>2600 Ma) affected by significant Paleoproterozoic magmatic
events. The study area is part of a CAP domain known as Roraima
Block. This block is completely covered by the 1980–1960 Ma
Surumu acid volcanic rocks and the overlying ca. 1870 Ma sedi-
mentary sequences of the Roraima Supergroup, that includes the
basal Arai Formation, the Suapi Group and the Uaimapué Formation
at the top (Fig. 1c) (Teixeira et al., 1989; Tassinari and Macambira,
1999; Santos et al., 2003). The Roraima basin is possibly related to
a N-S extensional event, responsible for the development of nor-
mal E-W faults and transference faults. It has been interpreted as
an intracontinental type basin with regional rhombohedral geom-
etry controlled by NW-SE system faults. Later, during the K’Mudku
Episode around 1.2 Ga the basin experienced a weak positive inver-
sion involving the reactivation of normal upthrow faults, where
the transfer faults worked as lateral ramps. At the southern border
of the basin along the Brazilian side, in the proximity of the E-W
faults, the Roraima Supergroup was affected by en echelon folds.
Towards the center of the basin, no deformation was recorded in
these rock units, suggesting their primary stratigraphic relation-
ships were preserved (Reis et al., 2012).
Mafic sills and dykes of the Avanavero magmatic event intruded
into the volcanic and sedimentary formations of the Surumu Group
and the Roraima Supergroup (Brito Neves, 2011; Reis et al., 2010,
2013). The Avanavero magmatism extends to the surrounding
countries of Venezuela, Guyana and Suriname, and forms a large
igneous province (LIP). The sills follow the original structures of the
Roraima sedimentary rocks, i.e., their bedding planes. In the study
area these structural planes have northwest-southeast strikes and
dip to northeast between 5◦ and 20◦ (Fig. 1c). Groeneweg and
Bosma (1969) were the first to use the name Avanavero to des-
ignate dolerite dykes and large irregular sheet-shaped bodies in
the Avanavero area and other locations in Suriname. In Brazil, this
Proterozoic basic magmatism comprises four levels of sills that are
informally called Cotingo, Camararém, Paiuá and Pedra Preta sills
(Pinheiro et al., 1990). The Cotingo sill intrudes the Surumu volcanic
rocks. It is about 140 km long and 40 m thick and strikes WNW-
ESE. A small sill near the contact between the Surumu volcanics
and the Arai sandstones is known as Camararém sill. It extends
northwards to the Guyanas where it is known as Tumatumari sill.
Sill Camararém is 30 meters thick and follows the orientation of
the host sedimentary rocks dipping 20◦ to northeast (see Fig. 1c).
Paiuá sill is 20 m thick. It cuts quartz sandstones at the first 200
meters of the Arai Formation and dips ca. 15◦to the northeast (see
Fig. 1c). Finally, the Pedra Preta sill cuts across the Suapi Group,
where siltstones near the contact with the mafic rock were horn-
felsed (Pinheiro et al., 1990). A thickness of about 250 meters is
estimated for this sill that shows a gentle dip of around 12◦to the
northeast (Fig. 1c). Basic dykes associated with major faults (NE
and NW trends) in the Roraima Supergroup are interpreted as the
feeders of the poorly differentiated Avanavero dolerite sills. Meso-
zoic basic dykes associated with major mainly NE faults cut all the
Proterozoic rocks (Reis et al., 2004).
The Avanavero rocks comprise dark-gray medium to coarse
grained dolerites and gabbros, and subordinately by
and
microdiorites
micro-quartz diorites (Reis et al., 2013). Under the micro-
scope they are composed of plagioclase, pyroxene and amphibole,
with magnetite and ilmenite as accessory minerals. Late hydro-
thermal processes are common, such as alteration of plagioclase
to clay minerals and/or albite (Pinheiro et al., 1990). Dolerite dykes
show generally subophitic texture, and are composed of plagio-
clase (labradorite), pyroxene (augite and occasionally pigeonite),
hornblende and chlorite. Sericite and epidote appear as accessory
minerals (Reis et al., 2013).
U–Pb ages in baddeleyite were obtained for several dolerite
dykes and sills of the Avanavero magmatic suite. These comprise
ages of 1794 ± 4 Ma for a dolerite intrusive into the Omai gold
deposit in Guyana (Norcross et al., 2000), a 1787 ± 14 Ma age for the
Cipó dolerite and a 1782 ± 3 Ma age for the Cotingo dolerite (Santos
et al., 2003). Similar ages were also obtained for correlative mafic
intrusions in Pará and Amazonas Brazilian States, located several
hundreds of kilometers south of the studied area. They comprise a
1780 ± 7 Ma age for the Crepori sill in southwest Pará State, and a
1780 ± 3 Ma age for the Quarenta Ilhas sill in northeast Amazonas
State (Santos et al., 2002). Recently, Reis et al. (2013) presented two
new U–Pb baddeleyite ages for Avanavero rocks: a 1795 ± 2 Ma age
for the Pedra Preta sill, and a 1793 ± 2 Ma age for a dolerite sill cross-
cutting the Urupi Formation (Central-Brazil Shield), whose rocks
have been correlated with those from the Roraima Supergroup. A
mean age of 1788.5 ± 2.5 Ma was calculated from all U–Pb ages and
is assumed to be the best age estimate for the Avanavero magmatic
event. Besides,40Ar–39Ar analysis on biotite of a dolerite located
in Guyana yielded an integrated age of 1798 ± 2 Ma (Onstott et al.,
1984) that is in agreement with the U–Pb ages dataset. This age and
the fact that the Arai Group show only anchimetamorphic mineral
assemblages are strong evidence that the region was not submitted
to temperatures higher than 300◦C after the emplacement of the
Avanavero sills.
3. Sampling and methods
Paleomagnetic sampling was performed around the small vil-
lage of Uiramutã at the northern Roraima State (Brazil) where 118
standard oriented cylindrical cores were taken from 19 sites of four
well-exposed sills (Cotingo, Camararém, Paiuá and Pedra Preta)
from the Avanavero suite (Fig. 1, Table 1). From the Pedra Preta
sill, estimated to be 250 m thick, we sampled 7 sites (#1 to #5,
#18, #19 in Table 1 and Fig. 1) at different levels of the sill. Three
sites (#6, #7 and #8) were sampled from the Paiuá sill, estimated
to be 20 m thick. Four sites were sampled from the Camararém sill,
estimated to be 30 m thick, and five sites (#13 to #17) from the ca.
40 m thick Cotingo sill. Samples were oriented using both sun and
magnetic compasses. A baked contact test was attempted at site
#6 at the border of the Paiuá sill with host sandstones (Fig. 2). At
this point, the Paiuá sill is covered by six meters of sandstones dip-
ping 15◦to the northeast. In addition to the 8 cylinders collected in
the sill, we have sampled six oriented cores from the sediments at
the following distances from the contact: 300 cm (FR11-I), 326 cm
(FR11-J), 366 cm (FR11-K), and 516 cm (FR11-L, FR11-M, FR11-N)
(Fig. 2).
At the laboratory, cylindrical cores were cut into 2.2 cm height
specimens. Step-wise alternating magnetic field (AF) and thermal
demagnetization techniques were employed to separate the char-
acteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) component carried by
the samples. Steps of 2.5 mT (up to 15 mT) and 5 mT (15–100 mT)
were employed for AF demagnetization using a 2-axis tumbler Mol-
spin AF demagnetizer. Thermal demagnetization was performed
using a Magnetic Measurements TD-60 furnace in steps of 50◦C
(from 150◦C up to 500◦C) and 20◦C (from 500◦C up to 600◦C).
Remanent magnetization measurements were carried out using

JR-6A spinner magnetometer (AGICO, Czech Republic). These
instruments are housed in a magnetically-shielded room with
ambient field <1000 nT. Magnetic components for each specimen
were identified in orthogonal plots (Zijderveld, 1967), and calcu-
lated using the principle component analysis (Kirschvink, 1980).
At least 4 demagnetization steps were used to calculate vectors
using least-squares fits, and an upper limit for mean angular devi-
ation (MAD) of 8◦was used. Fisher’s (1953) statistics was used to
calculate site mean directions and the paleomagnetic pole.
Magnetic mineralogy was investigated through acquisition of
isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) in a pulse magnetizer
(Magnetic Measurements), and hysteresis curves using a MicroMag
VSM – Model 3900 (Princeton Measurements Corporation). These
curves give bulk coercive force (Hc), saturation magnetization (Ms),
and saturation isothermal remanence (Mrs), after subtraction of
the paramagnetic contribution from the high field portion of the
curve. Coercivity of remanence (Hcr) was obtained using the same
Micromag VSM instrument. Also, thermomagnetic curves (low-
field magnetic susceptibility versus (high and low) temperature)
were performed for several samples to characterize the magnetic
carriers in the rock, using a CS-4 apparatus coupled to the KLY-
4S Kappabridge instrument (AGICO, Czech Republic). Thin and
polished sections were microscopically investigated under trans-
mitted and reflected light, respectively.
4. Paleomagnetic results
NRM intensities vary between 0.975 A/m and 459 A/m, which
are typical values for basaltic rocks, with high contribution of
ferrimagnetic minerals. Stable characteristic remanent magnetiza-
tion (ChRM) directions were isolated after both AF and thermal
demagnetizations of 153 samples from 13 out of the 19 analyzed
sites. Scattered secondary components were removed in fields
up to 20–30 mT, and in temperatures up to 540◦C, after which
southeastern directions with low to moderate upward/downward
inclinations were disclosed (Fig. 3).
As for the remaining sites, three of them (sites #7, #8 and #12
in Table 1) presented a northern direction with low to moderate
downward inclination. This component is similar to that found for

Jurassic (∼200 Ma) dolerites collected in Suriname (South America)
by Veldkamp et al. (1971) suggesting these rocks are younger or
were remagnetized by this Permo-Triassic magmatic event. Sam-
ples from site #10 yielded northwestern directions with upward
inclination not far from the present-day geomagnetic field. Sam-
ples from sites #11 and #13 yielded unstable behavior after AF and
thermal treatment. Results from these 6 sites were excluded from
the mean directions and paleomagnetic pole determinations.

5. Magnetic mineralogy
Under alternating magnetic field (AF) treatment all samples pre-
sented mean destructive fields of less than 20 mT, but two distinct
coercivity distributions can be observed: (i) for some samples the
intensity of magnetization falls to less than 5% of the NRM before
20 mT demagnetization (samples FR11-C2 and FR145-A4 in Fig. 5a),
whereas (ii) other samples preserve more than ∼10% of the total
intensity at fields as high as 100 mT (samples FR4-F2 and FR1-D3 in
Fig. 5a). The low-coercivity magnetic grains are usually associated
with secondary components, while moderate and high coercivity
magnetic grains represent the ChRM isolated in the samples. Ther-
mal demagnetization showed two types of unblocking temperature
spectra: (i) a more common discrete spectrum, where unblock-
ing temperatures are limited to the range between 500–550◦C and
600◦C (samples FR2-B5, FR3-D2 and FR88-E1 in Fig. 5b) and (ii) a
distributed spectrum, where it is possible to distinguish two wide
ranges of unblocking temperatures between 0◦C and 450–500◦C
and between 500◦C and 600◦C (sample FR85-C4 in Fig. 5b). The
characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) is normally associ-
ated with the highest unblocking temperatures, whose magnetic
carriers are represented by Ti-poor titanomagnetite, as shown by
the decay intensity curves.
Isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) acquisition curves
for all samples are very similar, giving saturation fields of less than
300–400 mT (Fig. 5c). These coercivities are typical of magnetite or
titanomagnetite minerals. Narrow-waisted hysteresis curves were
obtained for samples from all sites, giving coercivities between
4.3 mT and 24.9 mT, also typical of (titano)magnetite grains. In the
Day’s plot (Day et al., 1977, modified after Dunlop, 2002) most
samples fall into the pseudo-single domain (PSD) field, or along
a trend parallel to the theoretical SD/MD mixing curves of Dunlop
(2002) (Fig. 5d). This is consistent with the stable ChRM directions
disclosed by thermal and AF treatment.
Both reversible and irreversible high-temperature (20–700◦C)
thermomagnetic curves were obtained, most of them with a pro-
nounced Hopkinson peak and a strong decay in susceptibility at
around ∼580◦C (Fig. 5e and f). Low-temperature thermomagnetic
curves show a susceptibility peak at around −150◦C denoting
the Verwey transition. These characteristics are typical of low-
Ti titanomagnetite grains (Dunlop and Ozdemir, 1997), which
are the main magnetic carriers of ChRM direction in the studied
rocks.
6. Petrography
Petrographic analyses were performed in samples with consis-
tent ChRM directions and also in samples showing unstable
inconsistent
and/or
directions. Mineralogical compositions and textures
observed in thin and polished sections for samples with differ-
ent magnetic behavior typically show differences that may explain
their contrasting paleomagnetic results.
Samples with stable magnetization show subophitic textures,
consisting predominantly of plagioclase (ca. 50–55%), augite
(35–40%), biotite (2–5%), opaque minerals (2–5%), hornblende (<
1%) and epidote (< 1%). Some samples (FR4-F1, FR5-G1, FR85-B1,
FR144-C3, and FR145-A1) show hornblende rims replacing augite,
and occasionally myrmekite (samples FR1-B1 and FR4-F1). In pol-
ished section, the preserved euhedral magnetite crystals (Fig. 6A
and B) are interpreted as the carriers of the ChRM. Minor quantities
of hematite and martite (Fig. 6C) are present and probably result
from late magmatic oxidation, but do not contribute significantly
as remanence carriers of the ChRM. Occasionally, anhedral crystals
of magnetite or hematite are observed as intergranular growths.
Locally, magnetite grains present fine ilmenite lamellae, diagnos-
tic of high-temperature oxidation-exsolution processes (Fig. 6B).
Magnetite is rarely observed in thin-sections of samples FR143-A1,
FR144-C3, and FR145-A1, although it is the main magnetic carrier
of the ChRM direction.
Samples with unstable magnetization consist predominantly
of plagioclase (ca. 50–55%), hornblende (10–20%), augite (0–20%),
quartz (0–10%), biotite (5–10%), and opaque minerals (5–10%). Thin
and polished sections indicate features typical of hydrothermal
processes, such as hornblende appearing as alteration rims in augite
crystals or in opaque minerals such as hematite (Fig. 6D). More-
over, a higher percentage of myrmekitic textures is observed in
these samples. Opaque mineral are predominantly hematite, mar-
tite, and locally preserved magnetite (Fig. 6E). Corrosion features
(Fig. 6D) are frequent in these samples, which could be the result
of dissolution of (or substitution by) new minerals (hornblende
or biotite). Martite crystals present patches or venules of thick
ilmenite (Fig. 6F).
In addition to the mafic intrusions, we have also examined thin-
sections from the host sandstones close and away of the baked
contact in site #6. Close to the contact the sandstones show mag-
netite crystals with skeleton forms (Fig. 7A), sometimes partially
replaced by martite (Fig. 7B). Away from the contact, martite replac-
ing magnetite grains and hematite as cement are more frequent
(Fig. 7C and D).
7. Baked contact test
Fig. 8 shows the demagnetization behavior of samples collected
at the Paiuá mafic sill and its host sandstones. Mean directions
for the sill (Dm= 151.4◦; Im= 26.6◦, ˛ =
95
4.7◦) and the sandstones
away from the contact (Dm= 3.6◦; Im= 12.9◦, ˛ =
95
20.4◦) are indi-
cated in Fig. 9. Most sandstone samples collected up to 366 cm away
from the contact (FR11-I, FR11-J and FR11-K) showed a direction
similar to that found in the intrusion (Fig. 9a). In contrast, sand-
stone samples (FR11-L to FR11-N) collected 516 cm away from
the sill’s border showed a consistent north-northwestern magnetic
component with low inclination (Figs. 8 and 9). The age of the
characteristic component of the sandstones away from the contact
is still unconstrained. These directions are close to the magnetic
components found in Jurassic dolerite dykes of the Guiana Shield
(Veldkamp et al., 1971; Théveniaut et al., 2006), and may thus rep-
resent a younger remagnetization of the sandstones. Some sites on
the mafic sills collected in the present study also provided similar
directions (Table 1). But most sites in the sills were not affected by
this thermal event. The fact that Ar–Ar dates on biotite are similar
to the crystallization ages of the sills also suggest that the region
has never been heated above 300◦C after the Avanavero magma-
tism. So, any remagnetization must be of chemical origin, related to

fluid circulation at the time of the Jurassic Central Atlantic Province
magmatism. This younger event likely affected the magnetic min-
eralogy of the sandstones away of the contact, as indicated by the
higher degree of martitization and hematitization observed in pol-
ished sections (Fig. 7C and D). IRM acquisition curves for samples
close and far from the sill confirm these findings, with those close
to the contact showing a normally smaller contribution of hematite
when compared with those away from the intrusion (Fig. 9b). Hys-
teresis loops for the sediments are wasp-waisted as a result of the
mixture between high- and low-coercivity phases (Fig. 9c and d).
Coercivities for samples close to the contact vary between 6.5 and
7.9 mT, whereas those collected away from the contact show higher
coercivities between 7.2 and 30.9 mT. In any case, if a Jurassic event
has affected the porous sediments away from the baked contact,
it seems to have spared the remanence of the sill and
close
sediments
to its contact, suggesting that both the magmatic rock and
the nearby sedimentary host kept the magnetic record of the time
of the intrusion.
8. Discussion
8.1. The Avanavero paleomagnetic pole
Stable southeastern directions with low downward and upward
inclinations (AV component) were disclosed in samples from the
Avanavero sills. Magnetic experiments indicate that pseudo-single
domain magnetite grains with moderate to high coercivities and
high unblocking temperatures carry the AV component, attest-
ing to its high magnetic stability through time. Although the
baked contact test cannot be considered positive, since the primary

nature of the magnetic component found for the host sandstones
cannot be proved, the magnetic mineralogy, petrography and ther-
mochronology described above together with the fact that the
Avanavero pole does not match younger poles for the region, sug-
gest the Avanavero ChRM direction likely represents a thermore-
manent magnetization acquired during the cooling of mafic sills.
Since only four sills were sampled a question arises if sec-
ular variation was eliminated. The angular dispersion (s = 18.2◦)
obtained in the Avanavero collection is compatible with an ade-
quate sampling of geomagnetic secular variation. However, this
dispersion may be related to later tilting that affected the sills.
The intracratonic ca. 1200 Ma K’Mudku tectonic event affected the
area to the SE of the Avanavero event (Cordani et al., 2010). It
is considered to have been developed under low (to moderate)
temperature conditions, and follows pre-existing E-W to NE-SW
structural features that affected the country rocks at Paleoprotero-
zoic times (Fraga et al., 2009). In spite of its regional importance
in central Amazonia, this event did not affect the studied sills.
described
As
above, the structural planes of the Roraima sedimentary
rocks in the study area dip gently to the northeast, with inclinations
increasing from northeast (dip of 5◦) to southwest (dip of about
20◦). Using the related structural dips at each collected sill, bedding
plane corrections for each related sill were performed. A new site
mean direction was calculated (Dm= 139.5◦; Im= −2.0◦; ˛ =
95
13.0◦;
K = 11.2), which differs by only one degree in declination and incli-
nation from the mean direction obtained before bedding correction.
The Avanavero ChRM directions are similar to those found for the
Aro and Guaniamo dykes from Venezuela, dated at 1820 ± 20 Ma
(Onstott et al., 1984), which are located ca. 600 km away from our
sampling area. The similarity in the obtained poles suggests that no
significant tilting affected the region.
If the sills were not greatly affected by tilting as shown above,
the only possible way that site mean directions express the record
of secular variation is to assume relatively slow cooling rates for
the sills. The cooling rate of magmatic rocks depends of various
factors, such as the thickness of the intrusion, its composition, and

the temperature contrast to the host rock. Simple thermal conduc-
tion models provide crude estimations on the time of cooling of
igneous intrusions (Jaeger, 1968). It depends on the square of the
half-tickness of the intrusion. For the Avanavero sills, the complete
cooling of the intrusions considering their thickness would be of
∼100 years for Paiuá, Camararém and Cotingo, and 5000 years for
Pedra Preta. It is worth noting that each sill has intruded at different
depths into the sedimentary succession, along more than 900 m of
stratigraphic thickness implying different cooling rates and in con-
sequence different remanence blocking times. From the 13 sites
included in the Avanavero mean direction, seven are from the Pedra
Preta sill, four are from the Cotingo sill, one is from the Camararem
sill and one is from the Paiuá sill. The Pedra Preta sill, which con-
centrates most of the sampling sites, is the uppermost sill in the
stratigraphy (see schematic profile in Fig. 1). Such a large intrusive
rock would take at least thousands of years to cool. This is coherent
with the medium to coarse grain sizes of the Avanavero rocks (dia-
bases up to gabbros) as described above. Although the other sills
are thinner they intruded different levels in the stratigraphy and
likely record the field at different times. In this way, we believe site
mean directions shown in Fig. 4 represent records of paleosecular
variation which was averaged out in the general mean.
The Avanavero pole (AV: 27.9◦E, 48.4◦S, N = 13, A = 95 9.6◦,
K = 19.6) satisfies 5 out of the 7 quality criteria proposed by Van
der Voo (1990) as follows: (1) U–Pb dating on dolerites from sev-
eral sills and dykes yielded well-defined and concordant ages, with
a mean of 1788.5 ± 2.5 Ma, which likely represent the age of magne-
tization acquisition; (2) the AV pole was derived from a set of 153
specimens (13 sites) and has adequate Fisher’s statistical param-
eters (A = 95 9.6◦, K = 19.8); (3) remanence vectors were isolated by
least-squares fit from orthogonal diagrams (Kirschvink, 1980) after
stepwise AF and thermal demagnetization; (5) the Avanavero rocks
in the investigated area are situated in the Archean Amazonia-
Central Province, which remained stable during the
of
evolution
the Ventuari-Tapajós (1980–1810 Ma) and Rio Negro-Juruena
(1780–1550 Ma) provinces, and the ca. 1200 Ma K’Mudku event
seemed to have only slightly affected the Avanavero rocks at its
southern border; (7) similar directions are not found in young units
from the same region or cratonic block. Two criteria were not sat-
isfied: (4) the baked contact test is not complete since we cannot
prove that the direction found in the host rock far from the con-
tact is primary or older than that of the intrusion; and (6) only a
single polarity was found for these rocks. In sum, the Avanavero
pole (AV) may be regarded as a robust pole (Q = 5), and as such it
can be used to constrain the paleogeographic position of the proto-
Amazonian Craton at ∼1789 Ma and test the paleogeography of the
proto-Amazonian Craton in the Columbia Supercontinent.
8.2. SAMBA connection and Laurentia in Columbia
A paleomagnetic based reconstruction of the Columbia Super-
continent at ∼1780 Ma was presented by Bispo-Santos et al.
(2008). In their reconstruction Laurentia, Baltica, North China and
Amazonian Craton were laterally disposed along a Paleo- to Meso-
proterozoic subduction-related mobile belt at the western side
of the supercontinent (Fig. 10a). The position of the Amazonian
Craton in that reconstruction was constrained by the 1780 Ma
Colíder Group paleomagnetic pole. Recently, D’Agrella-Filho et al.
(2012), interpreting new paleomagnetic data from the 1416 Ma
Indiavaí mafic intrusive, proposed a very similar configuration
(Fig. 10b), but which incorporated rotations within Baltica. In
their model, Sarmatia (together with Amazonia and West Africa)
were rotated 43◦ counterclockwise about an Euler pole at 48◦N,
42.2◦E relative to the Fennoscandia/Volgo-Uralia block following
Bogdanova et al. (2008) and Elming et al. (2010). In their interpre-
tation, D’Agrella-Filho et al. (2012) placed the North China block
between Fennoscandia and Amazonian Craton, but suggested a
triple junction between Fennoscandia/Sarmatia, North China and

Amazonia; the break-up of North China and its drift away from
the supercontinent occurring at 1780 Ma ago. According to those
authors the profuse 1790–1780 Ma anorogenic intraplate magma-
tism in Fennoscandia, Amazonia and North China would be the
record of this rupture. They include: the 1780 Ma dykes of the Små-
land Province in south Fennoscandia (Pisarevsky and Bylund, 2010),
the 1789 Ma dykes and sills from the Avanavero LIP in northern
Amazonian Craton, and the 1780 Ma dykes widely spread in north
and south of North China (Kusky et al., 2007). Yet, even though the
Baltica/North China/Amazonia link was supported by the 1780 Ma
Colíder Group pole (Bispo-Santos et al., 2008; D’Agrella-Filho et al.,
2012), most authors consider that Baltica was directly linked to
proto-Amazonian Craton at that time, with no intervening block
(Geraldes et al., 2001; Zhao et al., 2004, 2006; Hou et al., 2008;
Johansson, 2009; among others). This model has received the name
of SAMBA after Johansson (2009), in a paleogeography of Columbia
where Laurentia, Baltica, Amazonia and West Africa Cratons formed
a great continental mass, which remained together for 500 Ma,

Ma.
new 1789 Ma paleomagnetic pole obtained for the
Avanavero sills allows us to test the SAMBA connection. Fig. 11
shows a reconstruction for Laurentia, Baltica, Amazonia and West
Africa Cratons using the following Euler rotation poles: 16.8◦N,
323.6◦E; −64.6◦ for Laurentia, 6.3◦N, 281.3◦E, −41.1◦ for Baltica,
56.6◦N, 152.9◦E, 80.1◦ for proto-Amazonia, and 9.6◦N, 182.7◦E,
93.4◦ for West Africa Craton. In this reconstruction, correlatable
geological provinces adjust according to the model of Johansson
(2009). Also, the Guri (in Guiana Shield, Amazonian Craton) and
Sassandra (in West Africa Craton) mega-shear zones are aligned
as suggested by geological and paleomagnetic data (e.g., Onstott
and Hargraves, 1981; Nomade et al., 2003; Evans and Mitchell,
2011; Bispo-Santos et al., 2014). Available paleomagnetic poles for
Laurentia, Baltica and Amazonian Craton between 1800 Ma and
1750 Ma are presented in Table 2, and plotted in Fig. 11 after rotat-
ing them according to rotation poles assigned for each continent.
For Amazonia, besides the Avanavero pole represented by AC-1,
Onstott et al. (1984) published paleomagnetic results (their com-
ponent II) for the Aro and Guaniamo dykes from Venezuela, which

2). This pole (AC-2 in Fig. 11) together with the Avanavero
pole (AC-1) may be used to trace a short APW path (between
1820 Ma and 1790 Ma) for the proto-Amazonian craton (Fig. 11).
Four paleomagnetic poles are presently available for Baltica
in the time interval between 1790 Ma and 1750 Ma (Table 2):
the Ropruchey sill (Fedotova et al., 1999), the Shoksha Formation
(Pisarevsky and Sokolov, 2001), the Hoting Gabbro (Elming et al.,
2009) and the Småland Intrusive (Pisarevsky and Bylund, 2010). A
U–Pb zircon age of 1786 ± 10 Ma is attributed to the Hoting Gabbro
but younger 1650–1610 Ma 40Ar–39Ar biotite ages for the same
rocks bring some uncertainties concerning the age of the Hoting
pole. Until recently the Ropruchey sill’s pole was constrained by
a U–Pb zircon age of 1770 ± 12 Ma (Fedotova et al., 1999) but a
precise baddeleyite age of 1751 ± 3 Ma recently obtained for these
rocks suggests a younger age for it (Lubnina et al., 2012). This is
consistent with the fact that this pole differs by some degrees
from the 1784–1769 Ma Småland Intrusions pole (Pisarevsky and
Bylund, 2010). The age of the Shoksha pole is constrained between
1800 Ma using a glauconite K–Ar age for the underlying Petroza-
vodsk Formation and the 1751 ± 3 Ma age of the Ropruchey sill that
cuts the Shoksha Formation. The agreement between the Shoksha
(BA-3) and Hoting (BA-4) poles with the well-dated Ropruchey sill
pole (BA-2) (Fig. 11, Table 2) strongly suggests these three poles
represent the Baltica position at about 1750 Ma ago. These poles
also agree (within error) with the Laurentian 1750 Ma pole, a mean
of nineteen post-Hudsonian poles with ages between 1760 and
1740 Ma calculated by Irving and colleagues (2004) (LA-1 in Fig. 11
and Table 2). In the Baltica/Amazonian Craton reconstruction pro-
posed here, the older 1784–1769 Ma Småland Intrusions pole (BA-1
in Fig. 11) matches within error the ca. 1790 Ma Avanavero pole
(AC-1) corroborating the SAMBA connection of Johansson (2009).
A similar Laurentia/Baltica/Amazonia configuration was also
recently proposed by Mertanen and Pesonen (2012) based on
1530 Ma paleomagnetic poles from Laurentia, Baltica and Ama-
zonian cratons. Although paleomagnetic data for West Africa
for this time interval is actually absent, geological evidence and
older 2100–1970 Ma paleomagnetic data corroborate the Amazo-
nia/West Africa link shown in Fig. 11 (Onstott et al., 1984; Nomade
et al., 2003; Evans and Mitchell, 2011; Bispo-Santos et al., 2014).
This great continental mass was probably the core of the Columbia
Supercontinent (Salminen and Pesonen, 2007). Its western margin,
formed by the contiguous Laurentia, Baltica and proto-Amazonian
craton, was the scenario of coeval Andine-type, subduction-related
accretionary mobile belts during Paleo- to Mesoproterozoic, which
formed the Yavapai-Mazatzal-Labradorian (1800–1400 Ma) in

Laurentia, the trans-Scandinavian-Kongsbergian (1800–1700 Ma)
and Gothian (1660–1520 Ma) in Baltica, and the Ventuari-Tapajós
(1950–1800 Ma) and Rio Negro-Juruena (1850–1550 Ma) in the
Amazonian Craton (Hoffman, 1988; Bettencourt et al., 1996;
Geraldes et al., 2001; Sadowski, 2002; Johansson, 2009; Mertanen
and Pesonen, 2005, 2012).
Recently, Pisarevsky et al. (2014) rejected the SAMBA model
and proposed that the Amazonia/West Africa never took part in
Columbia. In their model (Fig. 10c), subduction-related zones in
Amazonia/West Africa and Laurentia/Baltica correspond to oppo-
site margins of an ocean and have opposite sense. The main
reasoning for that is that Baltica was not yet completely assem-
bled at 1790 Ma (Bogdanova et al., 2008; Elming et al., 2010). In
a recent paper, Bogdanova et al. (2013) suggest an oblique colli-
sion of Sarmatia/Volgo-Uralia with Fennoscandia at 1800–1770 Ma,
and a posterior counterclockwise rotation of Sarmatia/Volgo-Uralia
to explain the 1800–1750 Ma mafic dyke intrusions related to an
AMCG suite that are widespread in the Ukranian Shield.
as
However,
stated by Bogdanova et al. (2013), ‘the presently available pale-
omagnetic data for 1.75 Ga are still too limited to decide whether
there was a wide oceanic gap between Fennoscandia and Volgo-
Sarmatia at that time, or whether that gap was much narrower or
even nonexistent’.
8.3. Avanavero pole versus Colíder Group pole
The Baltica/Amazonia link in the Columbia Supercontinent pro-
posed in Fig. 11 contrasts with the model proposed by Bispo-Santos
et al. (2008) and D’Agrella-Filho et al. (2012), based on the Colíder
Group pole, where North China would be placed between Baltica
and the Amazonian Craton.
The 1790 Ma Avanavero pole was obtained for anorogenic rocks
emplaced in an intracratonic environment (Guyana Shield, north-
ern Amazonian Craton), whose Archaean to Paleoproterozoic rocks
were only partially affected by the ca. 1200 Ma K’Mudku event
at its southern part (Cordani et al., 2010). As stressed above, the

Avanavero ChRM direction is likely a primary thermo-remanent
component. Meanwhile the 1790 Ma Colíder Group pole was
obtained for felsic rocks from southern Amazonian Craton, where
NW-SE magmatic arcs (forming the Jauru Terrane) were in progress
up to 1.32 Ga, with the final collision of the Paraguá Terrane
(Bettencourt et al., 2010). No field tests were performed for the
Colíder Group because of poor outcropping conditions. An easy
interpretation is that the Colíder magnetization represents a sec-
ondary component, and it cannot constrain the position of the
Amazonian Craton at 1790 Ma ago. In this case the SAMBA model
of Johansson (2009) could have prevailed at 1790–1780 Ma as indi-
cated by the Avanavero pole.
Alternatively, the Colíder Group pole could also represent
a primary magnetization. Its stable, high-coercivity and high-
unblocking temperature ChRM component seems to be carried
by primary magnetite and/or hematite (Bispo-Santos et al., 2008).
If both Avanavero and Colíder Group poles represent primary
magnetizations acquired at about 1790 Ma, then relative tectonic
movements must have occurred between the northern Avanavero
area and the southern Colíder area after 1790 Ma. Fig. 12a shows the
Avanavero and Colíder Group poles and the Amazonian Craton in
its present position. The Colíder Group pole is located to the west of
the Avanavero pole, and a rotation of 47.7◦of the Colíder Group pole
about an Euler pole at 23.8◦N, 327.6◦E (Fig. 12a), brings both poles
together. Approximately NW dextral strike-slip motions between
the northern Avanavero area relative to the southern Colíder area
could explain the different positions of these poles (Fig. 12b).
The Mesoproterozoic (ca. 1420 Ma) Nova Guarita (Bispo-Santos
et al., 2012) and Indiavaí (D’Agrella-Filho et al., 2012) poles from
southern Amazonian Craton are also plotted to the west of the
1460–1420 Ma poles from Baltica and Laurentia in the SAMBA
model (Johansson, 2009) (Table 3, Fig. 12c). This suggests that most
of these movements, if they occurred, must have happened after
1420 Ma ago.
The recent recognition of the Trincheira ophiolite (see topic 2) at
the southwestern edge of the Amazonian block suggests the dock-
ing of the Paraguá block to the proto-Amazonian craton along the
Alto Guaporé Belt to have occurred at the Middle Mesoproterozoic,
between ∼1470 and 1320 Ma (Bettencourt et al., 2010; Rizzotto
and Hartmann, 2012). NW-SE lineaments (the Buiuc¸ u shear zone)
are observed to the east of the Trincheira ophiolite, their
rocks
mylonitic
being dated at 1466.5 ± 1.4 Ma (Ar–Ar in muscovite) and
1467.8 ± 0.8 Ma (Ar–Ar in sericite). These shear zones are inter-
preted as a result of the Rondonian-San Ignacio Orogeny (Almeida
et al., 2012), which culminated with the Paraguá block collision.
We speculate that if both paleomagnetic poles result from pri-
mary directions, reactivations of these faults can be, at least in
part, responsible for the NW-SE dextral movements implied by the
available paleomagnetic data.
9. Conclusions
This study presents paleomagnetic data performed on mafic
sills from Avanavero magmatism, northern Roraima State (north-
ern Amazonian Craton), with a mean age of 1788.5 ± 2.5 Ma (U–Pb,
zircon). AF and thermal treatments revealed southeastern direc-
tions with downward/upward inclinations, carried by moderate
to high-Hc and high-unblocking temperatures Ti-poor titanomag-
netite/magnetite. Directions obtained from the host rocks close
to the intrusion match the ones disclosed for the sills. Directions
obtained in sandstones far from the intrusions are different. But
we cannot claim for a positive baked contact test because the
directions of the host sedimentary rocks away from the contact
can result from a much younger remagnetization. The calculated mean direction (Dm= 138.2◦; Im= −3.4◦; N = 13, ˛ =
95
13.0◦) for the
Avanavero sills, yielded the paleomagnetic pole (AV pole) at 27.9◦E,
48.4◦S (A =
95
9.6◦), which can be classified with a reliable factor
Q = 5. The presently available Paleoproterozoic paleomagnetic poles
corroborate the SAMBA model of Johansson (2009), with a nearly
equatorial Columbia Supercontinent being formed by Laurentia,
Baltica, proto-Amazonian Craton and West Africa, although other
configurations are also possible (e.g., Pisarevsky et al., 2014).
